q: Name a software design pattern that is not one of the 23 in the Gang of Four book.
hint: Named patterns and idioms from catalogs like PoEAA, POSA, Enterprise Integration Patterns, DDD or cloud design patterns count. Singleton, Observer and the other GoF patterns do not.

answers.l: Devised by Trygve Reenskaug at Xerox PARC in 1978-79 for Smalltalk. The GoF book discusses it only as an example built from Observer, Composite and Strategy.
Martin Fowler coined the name in a January 2004 article to separate it from the broader term Inversion of Control.
Catalogued in Fowler's Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002) and central to Eric Evans' Domain-Driven Design (2003).
Senders publish to topics without knowing the receivers. It appears as Publisher-Subscriber in POSA1 and Publish-Subscribe Channel in Enterprise Integration Patterns.
Announced by Microsoft's John Gossman in a 2005 blog post as the pattern behind WPF data binding.
Originated at Taligent, an Apple, IBM and HP venture, in the early 1990s. Mike Potel described it in a 1996 paper.
Greg Young popularized it around 2010, building on Bertrand Meyer's command-query separation principle from Eiffel.
Stores every state change as an immutable event and rebuilds state by replaying them. Martin Fowler described it in a 2005 article.
Popularized by Michael Nygard's 2007 book Release It!. It stops calling a failing dependency until a timeout passes.
From a 1987 paper by Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem on long-lived transactions, with each step paired with a compensating action.
Reuses expensive objects such as database connections instead of creating new ones each time.
Bobby Woolf wrote it up in the Pattern Languages of Program Design series: an object with do-nothing behavior that replaces null checks.
Dijkstra posed the bounded-buffer form in the mid-1960s and solved it with semaphores. It decouples creating work from processing it.
Keeps worker threads waiting on a task queue. Java standardized one in java.util.concurrent with J2SE 5.0 in 2004.
PoEAA uses it to cut the number of remote calls. Sun's Core J2EE Patterns called the same idea a Transfer Object.
Named in Fowler's PoEAA (2002). David Heinemeier Hansson took the name for the Ruby on Rails ORM.
Fowler's 2004 article set it beside dependency injection. Mark Seemann later argued it is an anti-pattern.
Defers loading data until needed. PoEAA lists four forms: lazy initialization, virtual proxy, value holder and ghost.
A single entry point that routes client requests to backend microservices. Chris Richardson's microservices.io catalogs it.
Martin Fowler named it in 2004 after strangler fig vines he saw in Australia that slowly envelop their host tree.
Developed for C++ largely by Bjarne Stroustrup and Andrew Koenig. A resource's lifetime is tied to an object's scope.
PoEAA pattern that tracks objects changed in a business transaction and writes them out together. Entity Framework's DbContext implements it.
PoEAA pattern that keeps domain objects ignorant of the database. Hibernate and Doctrine follow it, unlike Active Record ORMs.
Popularized by Sun's Core J2EE Patterns catalog to hide database access behind an interface.
A single handler for all web requests. Spring MVC's DispatcherServlet is a well-known example.
Randy Stafford wrote the Service Layer chapter in Fowler's PoEAA. It defines an application's boundary and its set of operations.
A small object compared by value rather than identity, like a date range. Both PoEAA and Evans' DDD describe it.
Microsoft's cloud design patterns catalog recommends retrying transient failures, usually with exponential backoff.
Runs helper functions like proxies or log shippers in a separate container beside the main app. Istio injects Envoy this way.
Splits data horizontally across databases by a shard key. Microsoft's cloud design patterns catalog lists it.
The application checks the cache, and on a miss loads from the data store and fills the cache itself.
An architectural pattern in POSA1 (1996). Unix shell pipelines, added by Doug McIlroy's push in 1973, are the classic example.
Douglas Schmidt described it in the mid-1990s for demultiplexing I/O events. Node.js and Netty event loops follow it.
Broken in Java until the JSR-133 memory model fix in Java 5, as the 'Double-Checked Locking is Broken' declaration explained.
Allows many readers or one writer. Courtois, Heymans and Parnas formalized the readers-writers problem in 1971.
Friedman and Wise used the term promise in 1976. Baker and Hewitt introduced future in 1977.
Splits a task into parallel subtasks and joins their results. Java 7 added Doug Lea's ForkJoinPool framework.
Game architecture where entities are IDs, components hold data and systems hold logic. Unity's DOTS is built on it.
Processes input, updates state and renders each frame. Robert Nystrom gives it a chapter in Game Programming Patterns (2014).
Introduced by Mackinnon, Freeman and Craig in the XP2000 paper 'Endo-Testing: Unit Testing with Mock Objects'.
JavaScript idiom using a closure in an immediately invoked function to keep private state, widely used before ES2015 modules.
Eric Evans and Martin Fowler coined the term in 2005 for APIs built from chained method calls that read like prose.
C++ idiom that hides private members behind a pointer to an implementation class to cut compile times. Qt calls it the d-pointer.
Martin Fowler wrote about feature toggles in 2010. They let teams ship unfinished code that stays switched off at runtime.
Facebook's unidirectional data flow architecture for React, presented in 2014. Redux later adapted its ideas.
Alistair Cockburn described it around 2005 to isolate core logic from UIs and databases through ports and adapters.
A strategic pattern from Eric Evans' Domain-Driven Design (2003) marking where one model and its language apply.
Enterprise Integration Patterns (2003) catalogs it for routing and translating messages between applications. RabbitMQ is a common one.
An Enterprise Integration Patterns entry for where undeliverable messages go. Amazon SQS calls it a dead-letter queue.
EIP pattern using one channel for the request and another for the reply, usually linked by a correlation identifier.
The first architectural pattern in POSA1 (1996). The OSI model's seven layers are its textbook example.
POSA2 (2000) pattern for completion-based async I/O. Windows I/O completion ports and Boost.Asio follow it.
Decouples method calls from execution by queuing requests to the object's own thread. Described by Greg Lavender and Douglas Schmidt.
POSA2 pattern based on the monitor construct of Per Brinch Hansen and Tony Hoare. Java's synchronized methods follow it.
POSA2 pattern giving each thread its own copy of a global. C11 added the _Thread_local keyword for it.
POSA2 pattern for transparently plugging services into a framework. CORBA portable interceptors use it.
Eric Evans and Martin Fowler wrote it up in a joint paper. It packages a business rule as a combinable predicate object.
PoEAA pattern for a well-known object that other objects use to find shared objects and services.
PoEAA pattern that links implementations at configuration time instead of compile time, so they can vary by environment.
PoEAA pattern ensuring each row is loaded only once per session. Hibernate's first-level cache works this way.
The simplest domain logic pattern in PoEAA: one procedure per business transaction.
PoEAA pattern for an object model of the domain combining behavior and data, contrasted with Transaction Script.
PoEAA pattern storing a whole class hierarchy in one table. Rails uses a column named type for it.
PoEAA pattern that detects conflicting edits at commit time, often with a version column, instead of locking up front.
From Evans' DDD: a translation layer that stops a legacy or external model from leaking into your own.
Sam Newman wrote it up in 2015: a separate backend tailored to each type of client, such as mobile or web.
Named after a ship's watertight compartments. Michael Nygard's Release It! applies it to isolating resource pools.
Undoes completed steps of an eventually consistent operation when a later step fails. Microsoft's cloud catalog lists it.
Several consumers read one queue so messages are processed in parallel. It is in both EIP and Microsoft's cloud catalog.
Picks one instance to coordinate the others. Microsoft's cloud catalog lists it, and ZooKeeper and etcd are used to provide it.
Microsoft's cloud catalog lists it for precomputing query-friendly views of data held in another form.
Caps resource use per caller or tenant. Microsoft's cloud catalog lists both Throttling and Rate Limiting patterns.
Writes outgoing messages to an outbox table in the same transaction as the state change, then relays them. Listed on microservices.io.
Lets clients find network locations of service instances. Consul and Netflix Eureka implement it.
From Evans' DDD: a cluster of objects treated as one unit, with a root entity that is the only member outsiders may reference.
A DDD pattern for recording something meaningful that happened in the domain so other parts of the system can react.
EIP pattern that inspects each message and sends it to a channel based on its contents.
EIP pattern that collects related messages, usually matched by correlation identifier, and combines them into one.
EIP pattern that broadcasts a request to several recipients and combines their replies into one message.
EIP pattern for safely handling duplicate messages, which at-least-once delivery can produce.
EIP pattern that tags a reply with the ID of its request. The same idea is used to trace requests across microservices.
EIP pattern for a shared messaging infrastructure that lets separate applications work together.
Draw into a back buffer and swap it with the front one so viewers never see a half-drawn frame. A chapter in Game Programming Patterns.
An object hands a request to a helper object instead of inheriting behavior. Kotlin supports it with the by keyword.
An empty interface that tags a class with a property. Java's Serializable and Cloneable are examples.
Generalizes the singleton to one instance per key, kept in a map. It draws the same global-state criticism.
James Coplien named it in 1995 after seeing it recur in C++ code: a class derives from a template instantiated with itself.
Christian Heilmann described this JavaScript variant of the module pattern in 2007. It returns an object pointing at private functions.
A React pattern: a function that takes a component and returns a new one. Hooks replaced many uses after React 16.8.
Gerard Meszaros coined the term in xUnit Test Patterns (2007) for any stand-in: dummy, fake, stub, spy or mock.
Wraps a web page in a class so UI tests call methods instead of raw selectors. The Selenium project popularized it.
Bill Wake named this three-part test structure around 2001. It parallels Given-When-Then in BDD.
POSA1 architectural pattern for distributed systems where a broker coordinates communication. CORBA is the standard example.
POSA1 pattern separating a minimal core from extensions, borrowing its name from microkernel operating systems like Mach.
The Elm Architecture: a model, an update function for messages and a view function. Redux credits it as an inspiration.
POSA1 pattern where specialist modules work on a shared data store. It comes from the 1970s Hearsay-II speech recognition project.
An object refuses a request and returns at once if it is not in the right state, like skipping a save on an unchanged file.
Waits until a precondition holds before acting, as with calling Java's wait() in a loop on a condition.
POSA2 pattern where pooled threads take turns as leader waiting for events, then promote a follower and process the event.
POSA2 name for taking a lock in a constructor and releasing it in a destructor. C++11's std::lock_guard is the standard form.
PoEAA pattern with one controller per page or action, the model behind classic ASP.NET Web Forms code-behind.
PoEAA pattern that embeds markers in HTML to render data, as in JSP, PHP and ERB templates.
PoEAA pattern where one instance handles business logic for all rows in a table. Fowler ties it to .NET's DataSet.
PoEAA pattern with one object acting as gateway to a whole table and holding all its SQL.
PoEAA pattern with one object per row exposing its fields but no domain logic, unlike Active Record.
PoEAA pattern mapping each class in a hierarchy to its own table. JPA calls this the JOINED strategy.
PoEAA pattern with one table per concrete class. JPA calls this TABLE_PER_CLASS.
PoEAA pattern representing a database query as an object. Hibernate's Criteria API is an example.
PoEAA pattern putting a coarse-grained interface over fine-grained objects to reduce remote calls.
PoEAA pattern for an object that wraps access to an external system or resource behind a simple interface.
PoEAA pattern: a base class for all objects in a layer, such as a domain superclass that holds the ID field.
PoEAA pattern pairing an amount with a currency and handling rounding without floating-point errors.
PoEAA's generalized Null Object: a subclass giving special behavior for cases like a missing or unknown customer.
PoEAA pattern that locks data at the start of a business transaction so only one session can edit it.
Microsoft cloud pattern: a helper proxy, often run as a sidecar, that sends network requests on a service's behalf.
EIP pattern that stores a large payload elsewhere and passes only a reference token through the messaging system.
Microsoft cloud pattern where a gateway fans one client request out to several services and combines the results.
Microsoft cloud pattern exposing an endpoint, often /health, that external tools probe to check a service.
Microsoft cloud pattern putting a queue between a task and a service to smooth out bursts of load.
Services react to each other's events with no central orchestrator. Microsoft's cloud catalog lists it.
Microservices pattern where each service privately owns its data store. Listed on Chris Richardson's microservices.io.
Ian Robinson described it in a 2006 article on martinfowler.com. Pact is a well-known tool for it.
Evans' DDD context mapping pattern where two teams share a small, explicitly agreed part of the model.
EIP pattern that breaks a composite message into separate messages, one per element.
EIP pattern for a central unit that keeps state and routes a message through steps decided at runtime.
EIP pattern that adds missing data to a message by looking it up in another system.
EIP pattern defining one common message format so each application only translates to and from it.
EIP pattern that copies messages from a channel to a second channel for inspection without disturbing the flow.
EIP pattern where the receiver explicitly asks for the next message when it is ready.
EIP pattern where a subscriber still gets messages published while it was disconnected, as in JMS durable subscriptions.
Game Programming Patterns chapter on deferring costly recomputation, like world transforms, until a flag says data changed.
Game Programming Patterns chapter on indexing objects by position, with grids or trees, to find nearby objects fast.
Lets a game define new types, like monster breeds, as data instead of subclasses. A chapter in Game Programming Patterns.
Puts behavior shared by a group of classes into one helper class that operates on them.
C++ idiom where public non-virtual functions call private virtual ones. Herb Sutter advocated it in his 2001 article Virtuality.
A test helper that hands out ready-made example objects. The name came out of ThoughtWorks projects.
From Meszaros's xUnit Test Patterns: shrink hard-to-test code like UI to a thin shell and move the logic somewhere testable.
Builds test objects with sensible defaults and chained overrides. Nat Pryce described it, and Growing Object-Oriented Software uses it.
React pattern where a component takes a function prop and calls it to decide what to render.
Dan Abramov popularized this React split in a 2015 article, then added a note in 2019 saying he no longer recommended it.
Martin Fowler described it in 2004 as a class holding a view's state and behavior. MVVM is a close relative.
Fowler's 2006 MVP variant where the view has no logic and the presenter updates it directly.
André Staltz introduced it with his Cycle.js framework. Android developers later adopted it.
iOS architecture splitting a module into View, Interactor, Presenter, Entity and Router, described in a 2014 objc.io article.
Nests MVC triads inside one another. A July 2000 JavaWorld article by Jason Cai, Ranjit Kapila and Gaurav Pal described it.
Core J2EE pattern that hides lookup and remote details of business services from presentation code.
Core J2EE pattern chaining pre- and post-processing filters around requests, as Java servlet filters do.
Core J2EE pattern wrapping entity beans behind a session bean to avoid many fine-grained remote calls.
Fowler pattern that channels events from many objects into one object, so clients register in a single place.
POSA2 pattern splitting synchronous and asynchronous processing into layers joined by a queue. BSD Unix networking is the classic example.
POSA2 pattern separating connection setup from the service that runs over the connection. Schmidt's ACE framework implements it.
POSA2 pattern passing a token with an async request so the initiator can match up the completion.
POSA2 pattern making the lock type a pluggable parameter so a component can run single- or multi-threaded.
POSA2 pattern where public methods take the lock and call private methods that assume it is held, avoiding self-deadlock.
Comes from the join calculus of Fournet and Gonthier. A body fires when messages have arrived on a set of channels.
PoEAA pattern that builds a logical page from domain data, then renders it to HTML in a second step.
PoEAA pattern that converts domain data element by element into HTML, as XSLT does.
PoEAA pattern for a central object that handles screen navigation and application flow.
PoEAA pattern that keeps a row's database ID in the in-memory object to tie the two together.
PoEAA pattern mapping an association between objects to a foreign key reference between tables.
PoEAA pattern storing a many-to-many association as a table of foreign keys to the linked tables.
PoEAA pattern mapping a small object into columns of its owner's table. JPA's @Embeddable does this.
PoEAA pattern that saves an object graph by serializing it into a single large object column.
PoEAA pattern keeping session state on the client in cookies, hidden fields or URLs.
PoEAA pattern keeping session state on a server, often in serialized form.
PoEAA pattern storing session data as committed data in the database.
PoEAA pattern defining an interface in a separate package from its implementation to break dependencies.
PoEAA pattern replacing a troublesome external service with a simple stand-in during testing.
PoEAA pattern for an in-memory table of data, like ADO.NET's DataSet.
PoEAA pattern that locks a set of related objects with a single lock.
PoEAA pattern where framework code acquires offline locks so application developers cannot forget to.
Microsoft cloud pattern placing a dedicated host between clients and services to validate and sanitize requests.
Microsoft cloud pattern giving clients a restricted token, like an Azure SAS or S3 presigned URL, for direct storage access.
Microsoft cloud pattern deploying backend services as geographically spread nodes that can each serve any request.
Microsoft cloud pattern deploying many independent copies of an application, each serving a subset of tenants.
Microsoft cloud pattern coordinating distributed steps as one operation, with a supervisor that retries or undoes failed steps.
Microsoft cloud pattern moving configuration out of deployment packages into a central store.
EIP pattern that puts out-of-order messages back into the correct sequence.
EIP pattern attaching a list of processing steps to a message, which each step reads to forward it.
EIP pattern routing messages in different formats through translators so they all arrive in one format.
EIP pattern for managing a messaging system with messages sent over a separate control channel.
EIP pattern where a request names the channel for its reply, like the JMSReplyTo header in JMS.
EIP pattern routing a message to a dynamically computed list of recipients.
EIP pattern connecting a channel to a service so messages can invoke it. Spring Integration has a component of this name.
EIP pattern connecting two messaging systems so messages on one are replicated to the other.
EIP pattern wrapping data in an envelope with the headers a messaging system needs, then unwrapping it on arrival.
Game Programming Patterns chapter: a base class offers protected operations that subclasses combine in one sandbox method.
Game Programming Patterns chapter on laying out data contiguously so the CPU cache stays useful.
Simulates multiple inheritance in languages without it by pairing two linked objects. Hanspeter Mössenböck described it.
Moves a class's attributes into a separate data class to limit their exposure and allow write-once fields.
POSA1 pattern for reference-counted shared objects, the idea behind C++'s std::shared_ptr.
POSA1 pattern where an aggregate object encapsulates its component parts and coordinates them.
POSA1 pattern for transparent interprocess communication between peer components.
POSA1 pattern adding a dispatcher that connects clients to servers by name.
POSA1 pattern for managing all the views a system offers, such as opening, tiling and closing windows.
Joëlle Coutaz proposed it in 1987 as a hierarchy of agents, each with presentation, abstraction and control parts.
Fowler's MVP variant where the view does simple data binding and the controller handles complex logic.
Evans' DDD context mapping pattern: a published protocol through which other bounded contexts use a subsystem.
Evans' DDD context mapping pattern where a downstream team simply adopts the upstream team's model.
MVC variant where the adapter mediates all communication and the model and view never talk directly.
POSA2 pattern wrapping low-level C APIs, such as sockets and threads, in cohesive object-oriented classes.
POSA2 pattern letting an application link and unlink components at runtime without restarting.
POSA2 pattern exporting several interfaces per component, as COM does with QueryInterface.

nope.Singleton: One of the 23 Gang of Four patterns.
nope.Observer: Gang of Four pattern. Publish-Subscribe counts, Observer does not.
nope.Factory Method: Gang of Four pattern, as is Abstract Factory.
nope.Adapter: Gang of Four pattern. Hexagonal's Ports and Adapters counts.
nope.Facade: Gang of Four pattern. Remote Facade and Wrapper Facade count.
nope.Builder: Gang of Four pattern. Test Data Builder counts.
nope.Microservices: An architectural style, not a single named pattern.
nope.SOLID: A set of design principles, not a pattern.

traps.q: Which pattern did Trygve Reenskaug devise at Xerox PARC for Smalltalk in the late 1970s?
traps.l: Reenskaug wrote the first MVC notes in 1978-79 while visiting Xerox PARC.

traps.q: Which pattern did Martin Fowler name in 2004 after vines he saw in an Australian rainforest?
traps.l: The vines grow around a host tree until they replace it, as new code gradually replaces a legacy system.
